title: Everyone is an Intermediate Player

scoring.method: Points for each answer are added, divided by the maximum available points, and scaled to 100. Level ranges are inclusive.

tactics.label: Tactics
tactics.tip: Play one set with a single goal: move as a pair. After a good serve, return, or lob, look for the net together instead of making the decision independently.

technique.label: Technique
technique.tip: Use the same racquet regularly and prioritise control over power. Practise compact volleys at the feet, a reliable bandeja, and a soft chiquita before adding more smash.

perfectScoreTip: Nothing. Absolutely nothing. Please send match footage to verify this result—your group chat has some questions too.

levels.label: Beginner
levels.summary: The glass is winning more points than you are, but everyone starts somewhere. Keep the ball in play, stay curious, and prepare to fall in love with the lob.

levels.label: Beginner+
levels.summary: You know which end of the racket to hold and the walls are starting to make sense. Now turn those occasional good decisions into reliable habits.

levels.label: Intermediate-
levels.summary: The name checks out. You have the foundations, a few trusty shots, and at least one rally per game that makes you feel considerably better than this rating.

levels.label: Intermediate+
levels.summary: Your court sense is properly useful now. You construct points and defend the glass, but consistency and shot selection still separate your best rallies from the rest.

levels.label: Advanced-
levels.summary: You are no longer just hitting shots—you are building points. Tighten the weakest part of your game and your partner may finally stop giving you advice.

levels.label: Advanced
levels.summary: Strong decisions, reliable technique, and a healthy respect for net position. You are the person new players watch and quietly copy between points.

levels.label: Advanced+
levels.summary: Your padel brain is doing serious work. You read rebounds, manage space, and choose overheads with intent. Only the finest margins—and your ego—remain.

levels.label: Pro
levels.summary: Absurdly good court sense. You see patterns before they happen and make difficult shots look sensible. One tiny gap remains between you and total padel enlightenment.

levels.label: Bro You Tapia
levels.summary: Perfect score. Apparently you have soft hands, a galaxy brain, and a back glass that owes you money. Please take the rest of the day off.

questions.prompt: Do you serve and instantly run to the net no matter what?
questions.whyItMatters: Taking the net after serving is usually a good instinct, but moving under control lets you read the return instead of getting caught halfway.

answers.text: Yes—I sprint in every time, whatever the return looks like
I move in under control and read the return as I go
No—I usually stay back after serving
I honestly have not thought about my next move

questions.prompt: Do you have a preferred side—and do you know how to position yourself on it?
questions.whyItMatters: A consistent side helps you learn its responsibilities, cover the middle with your partner, and avoid hesitation when you need to switch.

answers.text: Not really—I just stand wherever I start
I have a preferred side, but positioning is mostly guesswork
I know my side and basic positioning, but switches can confuse me
Yes—I know my responsibilities and how to switch with my partner

questions.prompt: Your lob lands short and the left-side player has an easy overhead. What do you do?
questions.whyItMatters: A bad lob usually means an overhead is coming. Moving back together buys time and avoids being stuck at the net as easy targets.

answers.text: Stay at the net and hope they miss
Run forward to try to put them off
Move back with my partner and prepare to defend
Switch sides and leave everything to my partner

questions.prompt: You serve, and the returner lobs over your partner at the net. Who deals with the lob?
questions.whyItMatters: If the server turns back, the team loses its shape. Your partner covers the lob while you continue forward and keep the net position useful.

answers.text: I chase it from behind while my partner stays at the net
My partner turns to cover it while I keep moving toward the net
Whoever shouts first goes for it
We both turn and run back together

questions.prompt: You hit a good, deep return of serve. What is your next move?
questions.whyItMatters: A deep return gives you time to challenge the net. Moving forward with control turns a good shot into a better team position.

answers.text: Stay on the baseline and watch how the rally develops
Move forward under control and join my partner
Sprint all the way in without watching the next shot
Switch sides with my partner before doing anything

questions.prompt: Do you play with your own racquet, or do you usually rent one?
questions.whyItMatters: Using the same racquet builds a reliable feel for its weight and response, making soft shots, volleys, and overheads easier to repeat.

answers.text: I use a different rental almost every time I play
I own one, but I often switch models or am still getting used to it
I regularly use the same racquet and know its basic feel
I have my own racquet and know how it responds on different shots

questions.prompt: A fast ball comes at you at the net. What does your volley usually look like?
questions.whyItMatters: A short, compact volley gives the ball less chance to fly long or sit up, especially when there is no time for a backswing.

answers.text: I take a full swing and try to add even more pace
I can block it, but my volleys often float or sit up
I use a short, compact volley and usually keep the ball low
I stay compact and balanced, and can choose a punch, drop, or angle

questions.prompt: Can you aim your volleys at the opponents’ feet or into the middle during a match?
questions.whyItMatters: Volleys at the feet force opponents to hit upward, while the middle can create hesitation. Aiming low is often more useful than hitting hard.

answers.text: I mostly aim anywhere inside the court and hope for the best
I can aim there in practice, but not consistently in matches
I can reliably find the feet or middle in normal rallies
I can choose the feet, middle, or an angle based on their positioning

questions.prompt: Can you choose between different overheads, or does every high ball become a smash?
questions.whyItMatters: Different overheads solve different problems: a flat smash attacks an easy ball, while a bandeja or víbora can keep you at the net without forcing a winner.

answers.text: Every overhead is a full-power flat smash
I have a smash, but the kick smash, víbora, and bandeja are mostly theoretical
I can bandeja to keep the net and flat-smash easy balls
I can choose and execute flat and kick smashes, víboras, and bandejas

questions.prompt: Can you execute a chiquita—a soft shot that dips at the net players’ feet?
questions.whyItMatters: A good chiquita makes the net players volley upward, giving you and your partner a chance to move forward instead of staying stuck in defence.

answers.text: I am not sure what a chiquita is or have never tried one
I know the shot, but my execution is inconsistent
I can consistently play it toward their feet in matches
I can play it consistently and move forward behind it
